newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo 1996 trade gap seen above $2bn-Institute.
newsitem.headline: Yugo 1996 trade gap seen above $2bn-Institute.

text.p: Yugoslavia's trade gap will rise to well over two billion dollars by the end of 1996, the Institute of Economic Sciences (IEN) said on Wednesday.
"The trade gap is heading for $2.2 or $2.3 billion dollars, with exports hopefully reaching $1.8 billion and imports surging to $4 billion," chief IEN economist Stojan Stamenkovic told reporters.
Exports are stagnating, while imports are maintaining a dazzling upward trend, he said.
IEN refrained from giving forecasts on 1997 trade development, but said a rising deficit was not sustainable by the economy without foreign investment and genuine reform and privatisation.
Stamenkovic insisted the trade gap was a structural and long-term problem of the Yugoslav economy to be solved only with foreign capital.
"Our economy must have a trade gap, but the deficit should be covered by a surplus in the capital account. This means we must import capital," he said.
And capital will start flowing in only after Belgrade restores ties with the international financial community.
"Once the deal with the IMF is struck, it would signal to investors the level of risk is tolerable and the economy sufficiently stable for investment," Stamenkovic said.
In the meantime, the trade deficit is mainly financed from unofficial hard currency reserves -- bank accounts held by Yugoslav companies abroad.

Economists have difficulties to estimate the size of the capital, which mainly fled the country when the international trade and oil embargo was imposed in 1992. But they all agree unofficial reserves will have to dry up sooner or later.
